reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / consensus neurosarcoidosis guidance
clinicalPearls: Cranial neuropathy is the commonest presentation, with facial nerve palsy the classic finding, often bilateral
Basal meningeal involvement favours the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, causing diabetes insipidus and other endocrine deficits
Presentations are protean and include aseptic meningitis, myelopathy, seizures, hydrocephalus, and peripheral neuropathy
Only a minority have isolated neurological disease; most have systemic sarcoidosis providing an accessible biopsy target
Contrast MRI often shows leptomeningeal enhancement, dural masses, or parenchymal and spinal cord lesions
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating non-caseating granulomas while rigorously excluding infection and lymphoma
Corticosteroids are first-line, with steroid-sparing immunosuppression and anti-TNF agents for refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder in which an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response leads to non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. When the nervous system is affected, granulomatous inflammation tends to concentrate around the basal meninges and perivascular spaces, spreading along Virchow-Robin spaces into brain parenchyma, cranial nerves, the hypothalamic-pituitary region, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. The inflammatory infiltrate and secondary vasculopathy produce the diverse neurological syndromes seen, and chronic meningeal involvement can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow to cause hydrocephalus.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating disease
IgG4-related disease and other granulomatous vasculitides
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain and spinal MRI to map meningeal and parenchymal involvement
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, and exclusion of infection and malignancy
Serum and CSF angiotensin-converting enzyme with awareness of limited sensitivity and specificity
Whole-body imaging such as CT chest and FDG-PET to find accessible extraneural biopsy sites
Tissue biopsy demonstrating non-caseating granulomas with special stains and cultures to exclude infection
redFlags: Acute hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure from meningeal disease
Hypothalamic-pituitary failure with hyponatraemia or adrenal insufficiency
Rapidly progressive myelopathy with sphincter involvement
Diagnostic uncertainty where lymphoma or infection has not been excluded
reference.prognosis: Many patients respond to corticosteroids, but the course is often chronic or relapsing and some develop fixed neurological deficits; parenchymal and spinal disease and hydrocephalus carry a less favourable outlook.
pitfalls: Diagnosing neurosarcoidosis on imaging alone without histological or robust supportive evidence
Missing coexisting infection because granulomas can occur in tuberculosis and fungal disease
Under-treating and allowing relapse when corticosteroids are tapered too quickly
Overlooking neuroendocrine dysfunction in basal meningeal involvement
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
